before: We read in the church history that Eusebius wrote in Greek and Rufinus translated into Latin that in Gaul the bodies of martyrs were thrown out to dogs, and the dogs' leavings and the bones of the dead were burned up to the last bit of consumption, and those ashes were scattered into the Rhône River so that nothing at all would be left for any kind of memorial shrine. We must believe this was allowed by God for no other reason than so that Christians would learn, in confessing Christ, that while they despise this life they should despise burial far more. For if what was done to the bodies of the martyrs with such enormous savagery harmed them in any way, so that their most victorious spirits rested less blessedly, it certainly would not have been allowed to happen. So the thing itself made clear that the Lord did not say, "Do not fear those who kill the body and after that have nothing more they can do" (Matthew 10:28), because he would not allow them to do anything to the bodies of his dead ones, but because whatever they were allowed to do would do nothing to diminish the Christian happiness of the dead, nothing from it would reach the awareness of those living after death, and nothing would pertain even to the harm of their bodies themselves, so that they would rise again less whole.

before: It is by this wretched compassion I have described that those men are praised and blessed by King David who showed the mercy of burial to the dry bones of Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 21:12-14). But what mercy is being shown to those who feel nothing? Are we to drag back the belief that the unburied could not cross the river of the underworld? Far be this from the Christian faith. Otherwise things went very badly for that great crowd of martyrs whose bodies could not be buried, and the Truth spoke falsely to them when he said: Do not fear those who kill the body and after that have nothing more they can do (Matthew 10:28)—if those killers could do such great evils to them as to block their way to the places they longed to reach. But since this is beyond any doubt utterly false, and it does no harm to the faithful if burial is denied to their bodies, nor does it benefit the unfaithful if it is given to them, why then are those who buried Saul and his son said to have shown mercy, and blessed for it by a pious king? Is it not because the hearts of those who show pity are well disposed when they grieve over the bodies of the dead—bodies not their own—for things which, by that affection by which no one ever hates his own flesh, they do not wish to happen to their own bodies after death? And what they wish to be done for themselves when they will feel nothing, they take care to do for others who feel nothing, while they themselves do feel.
